Foreword

This booklet is compiled from the two most widely circulated Chinese charity texts. Although the content is not too profound or difficult to understand, it is extremely practical and beneficial knowledge in life, which can help people change their whole lives, or in the words of the ancients, "transform their destiny".

The first text is "Liu Pham's Four Instructions" or The Four Advices of Mr. Vien Lieu Pham, written by him to tell the story. of one's own life for one's children and grandchildren, and through it also clearly states the authenticity of cause and effect, advising people to be afraid to stay away from evil deeds and strive to do good. The second text is "Du Tinh Y's Enlightenment with the Divine Kitchen God" or The Story of Du Tinh Y meeting the Kitchen God, by Mr. Du Tinh Y recounting his turbulent life and a thrilling reunion with a character he firmly believes is the Kitchen God (or Kitchen God), thereby helping him look back at his own inner self to recognize and distinguish between good and evil things clearly

rhat, thanks to that, he was able to make the determination to "avoid evil and do good", and finally achieved the result of ending the series of disasters that continuously befell his family, so that he could live happily until old age. In other words, by changing his own mind, he turned misfortune into blessing.

Both texts clearly stating this “turning misfortune into blessing” were chosen by Master An Quang to be engraved and printed in the appendix of the book An Si Complete Book (Chinese version), placed right after the section Expanding the meaning of the essay Yin Essence. Master An Quang had many profound implications when choosing to circulate these two texts promoting charity, and the beneficial effect of this on readers has been clearly proven over time.

Regarding the first text, Mr. Vien Lieu Pham did not write it as a philosophical study, but as a sharing of practical experience, because he was the one who successfully applied what he wrote here. He truly transformed his destiny, changed his life from misfortune to happiness. It can be said, by the

Having worked tirelessly to save lives for many years, he succeeded in changing his own fate without asking for any supernatural power. He created his own destiny. And more than that, he asserted that what he can do, each of us can do if we have enough determination, without excluding anyone.

That is great news for all of us in this difficult and uncertain life: We can decide our own fate instead of just begging or settling. This proactive nature will certainly create a more optimistic and positive life. And that optimism and positivity is itself an extremely important quality for a happy, peaceful life. Therefore, even though more than four centuries have passed, Yuan Lieu Pham's advice is still valid, because the criteria of good and evil that he proposed seem to have been, are and will continue to prove correct in this life.

The Chinese version we use is the one engraved as an attachment

in the book An Si Toan Thu, put into the engraving by Great Master An Quang himself in 1918, that is, the ancient Chinese version, probably kept intact as when Mr. Vien Lieu Pham wrote it in the early 17th century. Currently there is another version called Lieu Pham Tu Huan Bach Thoai Thien (了凡四訓白話篇), is a text narrated by Mr. Hoang Tri Hai in a dialogue style. Because we want to closely follow the meaning of the ancients, we chose the ancient Chinese text.

There are currently 3 Vietnamese translations of this book. The first version by translator Tue Chau Bui Du Long, published in 2011, stated “reference refer to the printed version of Great Master An Quang”. As mentioned, Master An Quang chose to print the ancient Chinese version, so this note shows that the translator chose to translate from the baihua text and refer to the ancient Chinese version. The second Vietnamese translation of the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas Translation Committee, it is unknown what year it was published, but the version circulated on the Dharmasite.net homepage (the official website of the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas) clearly states that the source is translated from the Liu version Pham four teachings white legend. Vietnamese version

The third translation by Tran Tuan Man, published in 2013, is not recorded as being translated from any text, but based on the content, it follows very closely the dialogue text by Hoang Tri Hai.

Thus, all three existing Vietnamese translations are mainly based on the dialogue text. The dialogue has the advantage of being easy to read and understand for people today, but it has the disadvantage that sometimes there are inevitably subjective interpretations according to the translator's wishes, thereby distorting the meaning of the original work somewhat.

For example, in the ancient text, when talking about the virtue of humility and good deeds to accumulate virtue, there is a place written as follows: “須念念謙虛，塵塵方便” (cultivation and recitation of modesty, bare earth convenience...)

The dialogue of Hoang Tri Hai explains the meaning These 9 words become: “必須在每一個念頭 上，都要謙虛；即使碰到像灰塵一樣極小 的事情，也要使旁人方便” (must practice at every top of mind, do weak and humble, i.e., using banh dat, statue of foul dust, the most minimal thing, wild and weak use of people means...)

Based on the interpretation of the dialogue text, the Vietnamese translation of the City of Ten Thousand Buddhas translates as: “Every thought must be humble humble, every action must create a means for others, even if it is as small as a speck of dust, to devote wholeheartedly..."

Version by Tue Chau Bui Du Long The translation is: “often remind yourself that you need to be humble be humble even when it comes to very small things, for everyone you must also pay attention to be humble gentle..."

And Tran Tuan Man's version translates as: “in every thought must be humble; even if you encounter must Things as small as dust and ashes also want to make things easier for others..."

The common point of all three translations above is that they all understand the two words “tran and bare” (塵塵) according to the dialogue, as “像灰塵一樣極小” (statue of dust and dirt like the same minimal), and therefore both translate as “small as dust”, “really small”, “as small as ashes dust”...

But actually in ancient literature, using the two words “tran tran” (塵塵) here does not mean “small dust particles”, but implies a very large quantity, or in a more common way, countless,

immeasurable... Therefore, the above sentence must be understood as: “always maintain a humble heart, skillful use of countless means...”

This understanding is not due to subjective speculation, but has been encountered in many ancient texts. As in the poem Mong Trai Minh (夢齋銘) by To Thuc of the Song Dynasty, there is a sentence: “夢覺之間，塵 塵相授” (In between dreams, in the middle of the dream, in the space of a dream, in the middle of a dream thu - During a dream, there are countless things that go back and forth). Again, in Son Cu Bat Vinh (山 居八詠) by Thuong Dat of the Tang Dynasty, there is a sentence "塵塵祖彿師" (tran Tran Patriarch Buddha - countless Patriarchs, Buddhas...) Until the Qing Dynasty, Cung Tu Tran also had the sentence: "歷刼如何報彿恩？塵塵文字以為門.” (The kalpa is like a river to repay Buddha's kindness? Tran Tran Van Tu Vi mon. - After many lifetimes, how can we repay Buddha's gratitude? Countless written literature is the place to enter the Dharma.) Through this, it can be seen that the interpretation of the two words "Tran Tran" in the dialogue is not in accordance with the original intention, and the Vietnamese translations based on it are also misleading.

When making the version. In this Vietnamese translation and annotation, we are completely based on the ancient text and have very serious references and comparisons.

to clarify the meanings conveyed in the book. I hope that in the flower garden there will be more flowers and more fragrances, giving readers another means to learn the essence of the ancients.

Regarding the second text, we have not found any official Vietnamese translation, but we did find a movie based on the content of this text, presided over by Dharma Master Tinh Khong. This is a very thrilling story, recounting the unexpected reunion between a disgruntled Confucian student and the Kitchen God (Tao Quan), and the dialogue between the two sides shows us many important principles in distinguishing between good and evil, good and bad, and therefore also the cause that will lead to disaster or blessing. a typical example of turning misfortune into blessing. That is also the reason we chose to include his story in this book.

By introducing two true stories about characters that have been passed down through many generations, we hope readers will be able to receive the good implications of the ancients in recording and widely circulating these stories, thereby drawing valuable lessons for themselves in cultivating themselves towards goodness.

Even though this is desired, with certain limitations in the translator's capacity and qualifications, I'm afraid some errors cannot be avoided. Therefore, we look forward to receiving guidance from readers near and far, so that we can respectfully listen and make corrections in the next editions.

Nguyen Minh Tien

FIRST STUDENT LIEU PHAM

( LIEU PHAM TU HUNTERS )

Self-sufficient destiny

Childhood me lost my father early.1 My mother told me to give up my academic career to study medicine, because she thought that I could both support myself and help others. Furthermore, the fact that I studied and achieved a profession so that I could leave a name for the world was also my father's wish from a long time ago.

NOTE 1

Yuan Lieu Pham was born in 1533 and died in 1606. This text was originally written by him to teach his children, so some personal pronouns are used accordingly in the father-son relationship. When translating, we made a few minor edits to the way of addressing to make it more suitable for the majority of readers, because we consider that this does not change the main idea of ​​the text.

After that, one time I went to Tu Van Pagoda and happened to meet an old man with a long white beard and white hair, and an appearance like that of an old man. When I came to the respectful greeting ceremony, the old man told me: "You are a person in the royal family, one day you will definitely study for higher education, why don't you worry about reading books now?"

I immediately explained the reason. The old man said: "My family name is Confucius, from Yunnan, I received the Royal Algorithm from Thieu Tu. According to fate, I will definitely pass this technique on to you."

NOTE 1

That is, Thieu Ung or Thieu Khang Tiet, born in 1011, died in 1077, was a learned scholar, Having studied Zhou Dich for many years, he left behind many works such as Mai Hoa Dich Number, Hoang Ki Kinh The, Guan Qua Inner Heaven, Ngu Tieu's Question, Nhuong Son Tap, Tu Ba On's Farewell Story...

I immediately invited the old man home and presented everything to my mother. Later, considering what old man Confucius had predicted for me, it gradually came to pass. After meeting Mr. Confucius, I started to return to studying for examinations.

Mr. Khong again predicted for me about the exam path, saying that when I first went to school, the first time I took the exam in the district I would pass 14th, the exam in the government would pass 71st, the exam in the province would pass 9th. After I took the exam, in all three places I passed the exam exactly as he had predicted.

Mr. Khong again predicted my life-long fate, saying that by that year I would pass the exam. With such a rank, next year he will be chosen as a novice, next year he will be chosen as a tribute, 2 next year he will be appointed as a district magistrate in Sichuan province. After being an official for 2 and a half years,3 will definitely retire to his hometown, until he is 53 years old, at the hour of the Ox, on August 14, he will die at home, only regretting that he has no children. I took full notes of those things, always remembering them carefully in my heart.

Brief biography of Yuan Lieu Pham

Yuan Lieu Pham was born in 1533, formerly named Yuan Biao, later changed to Yuan Huang, given the title Khon Nghi, also had the self-name Khanh Vien; First he took the name Hoc Hai, then changed his name to Lieu Pham.

The ancestors of the Yuan family, who lived in Jiaxing prefecture, Zhejiang province, were an extremely wealthy family at the end of the Yuan dynasty. At the beginning of the Ming Dynasty, Yen King Chu Le usurped the throne from his nephew Chu Doan Van, proclaimed himself emperor, and proclaimed himself Minh Thanh To. At that time, some people protested and were captured and killed by Minh Thanh To. The Vien family's ancestors were also hunted down because they interacted with opponents. They were lucky enough to escape, so they had to wander everywhere, then came to live in Nam Truc, in Wujiang district, Suzhou prefecture, Jiangsu province.

During Yuan Lieu Fan's reign, he married a wife from Gia Thien district and then lived with his wife, but it turned out that he returned to his ancestral hometown, Gia Hung district, Zhejiang province.

Student Vien Lieu Pham paid great attention to the practice of meditation for health care. He left behind two famous works on this topic: Nhiep Sinh Tam Suc and Tinh Tu Tu Quyet. The book Essentials of Still sitting has 3 sections: Practicing, Practicing, and Regulating. Thien Du Hanh introduces the essentials of people practicing meditation, focusing on mind control, the system of attracting the mind, training the mind, calming the mind, nourishing the mind, and training the spirit. Thien Tu Vien discusses the self-experience of zazen. Thien Dieu Tien introduces 3 methods of controlling anger in Buddhism.

He wrote the book Liu Pham's Four Teachings around 1601 (69 years old). Initially, these were just teachings he wrote down for his son, Vien Thien Khai, who was just 20 years old at that time, so he called them Gioi tu van (Essay on teaching children). Later, the book was widely circulated everywhere, so later generations changed the name to Lieu Pham Tu Huan (Four Advices of Mr. Lieu Pham).

His father died early, and his mother advised him to study as a physician. Later, he met Mr. Confucius from Yunnan and taught him math.

Shao Kang Tiet's Royal Number and predict his lifelong fate. He listened to the Confucian family's advice and quit his medical profession and studied hard to gain fame and career. In the third year of Long Khanh (1569), he met Zen Master Van Coc at The Ha mountain, Kim Lang. The Zen master taught him the principle of doing good and accumulating virtue that can change one's destiny. He was like someone who suddenly woke up from a deep sleep. From then on, he changed his name from Hoc Hai to Lieu Pham to remember this meeting and the theory of self-reliance that he had just learned. From then on, he voluntarily decided not to fall into the ordinary way of thinking and doing things of ordinary people.

In the fourth year of Long Khanh (1570), he passed the bachelor's exam. In the 14th year of Van Lich (1586), he passed his doctorate, was appointed district commander of Bao De district, and later promoted to the position of Chief of Staff at Chuc Phuong Department of the Ministry of Infantry. He participated in the war with the Japanese army in Korea, and once commanded to repel the Japanese army.

In the 21st year of Van Lich (1593), on January 27, also in the war with the Japanese army that occurred in Korea, Ly Nhu Tung led the army at Bach De Quan and lost heavily. The Minister of Military Affairs at that time

is Thach Tinh, which advocates peace talks. Vien Lieu Pham agreed with Minister Thach Tinh's criticism of Ly Nhu Tung's military leadership. Therefore, Tung harbored resentment.

Some time later, Ly Nhu Tung complained to the court, charging Vien Lieu Pham with 10 crimes. Because of that, Lieu Pham was dismissed and returned to his hometown.

He died in his hometown in 1606. It was not until the third year of Thien Khai (1623) that his unjust case was clarified. He was posthumously awarded military merit by the Minister of Justice, Trieu Nam Tinh, and the court posthumously awarded him the title Thuong Bao Ty Thieu Khanh.

showed their determination to repent and reform themselves by changing their nicknames.

During the renovation process, Vien Lieu Pham followed the instructions of Zen Master Van Coc, applying the recitation of the Chuan De mantra to help calm the mind and support the avoidance of evil and doing good. Du Tinh Y himself realized the difficulty of self-help in changing his mind, so he put his complete faith in worshiping the statue of Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara and reciting his name 100 times early in the morning to ask for blessings, and thanks to that he always started a new day with a peaceful mind. In this way, he was able to maintain his determination to avoid evil and do good throughout that day.

To strengthen his mind to do good deeds, Yuan Lieu Pham applied the "excessive gong" method of his predecessors, which means recording all the good or bad things about himself so that he can monitor and recognize them for himself. Du Tinh Y also did the same, but due to his belief in the Kitchen God, he did this by writing down all the good and evil deeds in a note every last day of the month and burning it in front of the Kitchen God's altar to pay homage. Work

recording their own good and evil deeds has the function of helping them regularly review their past actions, thereby always living in awareness towards goodness. Therefore, both of these methods have proven to be effective, helping both people maintain a good mind and become better and better.

What both people have in common is that they believe in the existence of gods, a belief that belongs to folk beliefs and not to Buddhism. The Buddha taught cause and effect as a law that operates on its own according to the principle of "cause, effect", completely denying any reward or punishment of any supernatural force. What is worth noting here is that this difference does not create a contradiction in the beliefs of the majority of ordinary people, because they believe that whether the law of cause and effect operates by itself or is operated by God through the gods, the results are still the same, still based on the criteria of good and evil of the actions that humans have created.

The adaptability or skillful means of Buddhism is precisely at this point. Replace

Because of rigidly following Buddha's teachings in the Sutras, the patriarchs, when preaching Buddhist teachings, always knew how to adapt to the existing beliefs of the common people. Instead of creating conflicts by pointing out differences and refuting the belief - which can be called superstition - in God and gods, they cleverly led God or the gods already in the hearts of the people to become guardians of the dharma, widely spreading the truth of cause and effect. The teachings of the Kitchen God to Du Tinh Y are a very typical example. Therefore, Du Tinh Y's worship of the Kitchen God was no longer a blind belief, but it became an extremely effective supporting force in helping him avoid evil and do good. Because he himself did not have the strength to “cut off” all evil thoughts with one sword, so he relied on faith in gods. With the idea of ​​abstaining from fear because there is always a “spirit to prove monitoring”, he can always keep himself in a state of awareness, not allowing evil and evil thoughts to arise and control him.

We also see the same thing in Liu Pham's Four Teachings, when Vien Lieu Pham burned incense every night to report to God about what he had done during the day.

And the results of self-cultivation that both of them achieved proved that the adaptive means of Buddhist teachings were effective. Of course, once they have delved deeply into Buddhism, with a clearer mind, they will surely at some point clearly understand the law of cause and effect exactly as Buddha taught, without needing to rely on belief in God or gods anymore.

We can be confident that it is from this perspective of “skillful means” that Master An Quang endorsed and personally encouraged the circulation of these virtuous texts. Even though they are mixed with some folk beliefs that are not truly authentic, with the guiding power of the Dharma, these texts have brought benefit to many people, especially to the majority of the common people, most of whom do not have much knowledge.

Up to now, the promotional value of these texts can be said to have remained unchanged

. The evil and evil thoughts hidden in each person's heart always exist, and to overcome them to reform oneself is always extremely difficult. Therefore, the sharing of the ancients through this book is certainly still a valuable lesson for all of us on the path of striving towards goodness.

Moreover, the difficulties we face today on the path of self-improvement do not seem to be much different from those of the past. Mr. Vien Lieu Pham described it as “getting used to old ways”:

“... There are many people in this world who are intelligent and talented intellectual, but the reason they do not cultivate merit for deeply, do not develop good karma for widely, is just because they are used to following the routine. old, hesitant and timid, not determined enough... ... so just like that, he was infatuated for the rest of his life."

And the Kitchen God, when teaching Du Do, also said:

“... When he opened his mouth and let out a word, in his heart he still knew he was hurting good virtue, just because of old habits... ... couldn't stop.”

“Familiarity with old habits” or “old habits” are common diseases of most people. Buddhism calls these “old habits” habits and teaches that we must make efforts to eliminate them in order to achieve success on the path of practice. We can simply imagine the operation of habit energy like a car that has been started but then completely loses control. Therefore, the direction of the car is the previous direction, and it keeps rolling, unable to change. It is the inertia of a freely moving object. When it does not receive any additional direction changes, it will continue to move in the same direction.

This means that, if we are used to lying and have the habit of lying, then continuing to lie will be completely natural, without any effort or effort. And the same goes for other bad habits such as greed, theft, adultery, drinking alcohol, jealousy, anger... Therefore, self-improvement always requires a lot of hard effort, while indulgence in "following the old ways" plunges us into the evil

path without any effort.

That's why, Confucius once said: “Winning to win others is wisdom, to win yourself is the strong one.” (Winners pretend to be wise, conquer themselves pretend to be strong.) And in the Dhammapada, the Buddha taught:

“ Even on the battlefield,
Win thousands of thousands of enemies,
Win yourself well more,
Truly the ultimate victory.”

Dhammapada, verse number 103

translated from the Pali version

Self-victory is also a prerequisite for establishing one's own destiny, for turning misfortune into blessing. Therefore, it can be said that self-victory is the common goal of everyone who wants to improve themselves and change their lives for the better. And the starting point for such a fight to overcome ourselves requires each of us to objectively and accurately know ourselves.

Student Vien Lieu Pham, in his dialogue with Zen Master Van Coc, showed that he was quite aware of his own weaknesses, which he believed were the cause of some bad lives for him. Zen Master Van Coc agreed with his comments about himself and guided the way to "revolutionize oneself" as follows:

“... Now you know clearly your wrongs... ... so you must wholeheartedly repent, change yourself... All the things you have done before, seem to have died yesterday. End all things from now on will be as if new were born from today.”

This advice can also be applied to all of us who have had the good fortune to recognize our own mistakes. That is the determination to “erase and redo” life, completely break with the mistakes of the past and constantly strive to build a completely new beautiful future.

But Du Tinh Y's case does not seem to be so lucky. He endured much suffering but could not see the cause of the suffering, and therefore could not be satisfied with what happened to him. He blamed heaven and earth because he did not know his own mistakes. Why is that? Because his evil thoughts were mostly hidden in his heart and had not yet been revealed. Therefore, people can still respect him, see him as a righteous gentleman, highly virtuous... And from the respectful attitude of others towards him, he has returned to deceiving himself into believing that he "did nothing wrong".

Du Tinh Y's case seems to be the common case of many of us. It is not easy to recognize wrong ideas for yourself when they are still hidden in your heart, with nothing showing on the outside. A person may not have committed anything so that others can see him as greedy, selfish, lustful, violent... but that absolutely does not guarantee that he is truly a perfect moral person. A look accompanied by liking when encountering a beautiful girl, and followed by a thought of possessive desire, may not cause any attention or criticism

from those around, but actually sow evil seeds. If there are appropriate external conditions, no one can be sure that that starting point will not continue to develop into a flirtation, teasing, until it sinks deeper into a sinful act... The same goes for thoughts of greed, anger, jealousy, envy, bitterness, malice... They are like poisonous snakes that sleep peacefully and seem harmless in the mind, but always wait for an opportunity to rise up and kill all good things.

The scariest thing is that we cannot see that potential danger ourselves. Therefore, we even enjoy "weaving dreams" with evil thoughts such as greed, adultery, resentment... instead of trying to eliminate them as soon as they arise. We enjoy fantasies about lust, or thoughts of resentment against people we hate, or dreams of having property that is not ours... And when those things have not yet turned into real actions, we are extremely naive to believe that we are still "completely innocent".

Therefore, the teachings of the Kitchen God are not only for Du Tinh Y, but will also be extremely valuable if we know how to apply them to self-reflection. In the story of Ve Trong Dat, the text of Lieu Pham's fourth teachings quotes Lord Diem as saying: "One evil thought that arises is already evil, don't wait until you actually do it." This is completely true in Du Tinh Y's case and is also true of anyone's secretly harbored evil thoughts.

The ancient art of war has a saying: “Know others and know yourself, a hundred battles and a hundred victories.” In the fight to overcome ourselves, we cannot help but know ourselves. Self-reflection, examination, analysis and eliminating all evil thoughts that arise in our hearts from time to time is the most important and effective way to help us follow the example of the ancients in turning disaster into blessing. Hopefully everyone who reads this book will be able to do that.
